children.text: The video follows the pattern of her classic cooking video's, but the absurdity shines through in all aspects. Within the first ten seconds, Nara zooms in on herself instead of the recipe she is preparing. Her outfit looks to be off a runway rather than something a mom of four young children would wear. This allows Nara to send two decisive messages right as the video begins. First, there is a level of absurdity to the idealistic life she is portraying. Second, claims that she is a tradwife or lacking true self-expression cannot be taken seriously while she wears a Selezza London dress worth $1,164.

As with all her cooking videos, the stated reason for showcasing the recipe is simple; the kids asked. In this particular script, she states she would “make them some really quick” which is clearly sarcasm. However, much of the audience refuses to accept this. Knowing the response could be negative, Nara moves forward with posting the video in order to draw in multiple audiences. Not only does she have her Gen Z female fans that watch for the glimpse of luxury, but she maintains a reliable stream of haters that come from all walks of life. On top of the first two audiences, the TikTok algorithm continues to introduce people to her for the first time who then interact out of confusion. Just as each part of her recipe is thought through, unique lines in her video are meant for the wide range of people she can claim as her audience.

Instead of keeping the focus on the simplicity or accessibility of recipes, Nara consistently finds recipes that are technical and reduce the amount of processed foods used. This causes a distinct shift in the specific genre of cooking videos she produces. Her content loses some relatability with the largest demographic of cooking video consumers, but a certain niche of viewers that are heavily interested in holistic health become increasingly inclined to watch. Even though her stated goal is not to villainize the processed foods widely available to Americans, there is an underlying tone of superiority that comes with the “health” food genre which fits well with the luxury housewife aesthetic.

Almost four years into Nara Smith’s TikTok career she follows a similar pattern of video uploads. She switches between three to four main formats with varying levels of engagement. Before this video was posted, her most recent videos had underperformed based on past expectations. This likely provided the motivation for her to post a video where her technical cooking skills, humor, and lifestyle were all highlighted at once. Based on the production of the video, it is likely that Nara pre-filmed it long before it went up and was waiting for the timing to provide the greatest benefit to her through bringing back millions of viewers.

As any recipe progresses, there can be more physical work required to reach the final product. In most cases, people choose the path of least resistance. This is in direct disagreement with Nara's vision for her profile and persona. At this point in the video, she removes her $133 Selezza London gloves, puts them back on, takes them off, and then puts them back on. She has no need to pretend that what she is doing is normal. Instead, every extra step she takes toward her final product is simply an addition to the performance.

At this point, Nara re-emphasizes the amount of time and effort the skittles are taking, but her tone and visuals make it appear almost effortless. Unlike other video series where people attempt to recreate processed food products, she describes no frustration. In fact, she goes so far as to say that her children truly enjoyed the treat without complaining which most people would heavily doubt. The lack of authenticity, though clearly intentional, begins to move more of the audience away from enjoyment. While many content creators would view this negatively, the purpose of the video is to drive engagement. It does not matter if the ratio of hate comments to compliments is 100:1 if Nara can use it in the future to show her brand reach. This goes hand in hand with the use of rage-bait that is seen throughout most of her content. It is clear to general audiences that taking ten hours to make fourteen total skittles is unserious, yet it still activates enough of a discussion to benefit her.

The ending of the video is simple. Nara plates the skittles and states “both the kids and lucky love them”. If this was one of her earliest videos, this could be seen as a natural ending. Because of the flow of negativity surrounding her marriage, this comes off as a true statement. Nara did not start making skittles for Lucky (and if viewers pay attention clearly not for her children either), but she reaffirms her support in him with the simple ending. She does not abandon focus on her family because the audience holds it against her. Instead, she genuinely weaves it throughout her content.

Unlike many influencers and content creators, Nara Smith only consistently produces her content on TikTok and Instagram. However, this does not prevent videos from being heavily talked about on alternate platforms, such as X. This video was clipped and platformed on X where an additional audience was exposed to her. Though the cross-platform interactions are not immediately beneficial to Nara, they end up paying off in the long run. Each introduction of a new audience member, whether from X or another platform such as Reddit, increases her brand value and pushes her videos further. This opens opportunities for future collaborations, and greater compensation from the platforms she chooses to post on.
